name: Hassan Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. These are pictures of the future, not predictions. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy fresh fruit, vegetables and dried fruit for a wholesaler at the Eastfield market hub. My day starts at five, walking the pallets with the quality checker and tasting what's on offer. By eight I'm on the phone to growers in Spain, Turkey and Morocco, and the price changes by the hour. After lunch it's matching what the supermarkets and restaurants ordered against what I've actually got.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the market's noise and the feel of a good deal, like landing a pallet of apricots two days before the rival hears. What wears me out is the early starts, and food that spoils if I guess wrong. My wife Selin runs the office at a primary school, and we've got Deniz, who's thirteen, and Aylin, ten. The mortgage on our house is heavy, and savings are almost nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, a little help with the boring parts. I already use an AI tool to translate emails from the Spanish growers and to check a price against last year's. At work I'd tell the lads it's useful but it doesn't know a bad avocado from a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us it means keep the job and keep going. Nothing changes for my family, which is fine, but it's not great either, because our money is thin. Pay for buyers here is lower than in the cities, and there aren't many other wholesalers in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tool as I do, a few times a week, and be a bit more careful to check it. I'd keep my grower relationships warm, which is the real value. I'd try to put aside a bit every payday, maybe a hundred, into a savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. It's a world I understand, which is a relief, and I'm not scared. Just a bit stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The early hours. When Deniz had his school trip, I had to pay up front and hope the month would stretch. Under a month of savings means every price in the shop matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you carrying already that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad season. If the weather ruins a harvest in Spain, my bonus drops, and Selin's school wage is not enough on its own. That's what I'd worry about, not AI.

say: I'd tell the lads AI is **useful**, but it can't tell a bad avocado from a good one.
I'd say nothing changes much for us.
think: Nothing changing is fine, but our **money is thin** and local wholesaler jobs are few.
A weather-ruined harvest would cut my bonus and Selin's school wage can't cover it.
do: Keep using AI a few times a week to translate emails and check **prices**.
Put a hundred a **payday** into savings.
feel: **Okay**; I understand this world, though I'm stretched.
S0.quote: I'd tell the lads it's useful but it doesn't know a bad avocado from a good one.
fieldNote: Hassan is **uneasy** because of money and harvest risk, not AI.
He already uses AI a few times a week and distrusts its judgement.
His wife's school job is the household's steady anchor.

steps.text: Keep translating grower emails with the AI tool and check the results
Keep calling growers each week to stay close to them
Move a hundred every payday into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, let's see it prove itself. At the market everyone's got a view, so I'd tell the younger lads to learn it, because it's coming whether we like it or not. Online I'd say it needs rules on who gets retrained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think buying changes a lot. Matching orders to supply, spotting price swings, writing to growers: software could do most of it. I think the wholesaler goes from five buyers to three, and I'm among the best, but it's a risky thing to count on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every course the firm offers, and use the tools more, daily instead of weekly. I'd specialise in what a machine can't do: the quality, the talking with growers, the handshake. And I'd finally talk to Selin about a second small income for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled, but I'd cope. I've changed before, when the market moved to online ordering, and I came out okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What parts of your day could software do, and which parts couldn't it do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine could do the price matching. It couldn't taste the apricots or know that this grower's first crates are always the best. The people I'd worry about are the younger ones doing only the data entry, because that's the first thing to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the market?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn to look at the produce too, not just the screen. The ones who'll last can do both. I'd offer to show them the quality checks.

say: I'd tell the younger lads to learn it, because it's **coming** whether we like it or not.
Online I'd say it needs rules on who gets **retrained**.
think: I think the wholesaler goes from five buyers to **three**.
Being among the best is a risky thing to count on.
do: Take every **course** the firm offers and use AI daily instead of weekly.
Specialise in what machines can't do: **quality** and grower relationships.
Talk to Selin about a second small income.
feel: **Unsettled**, but I'd cope; I changed before when the market moved online.
S1.quote: A machine could do the price matching. It couldn't taste the apricots or know that this grower's first crates are always the best.
fieldNote: Hassan thinks the team could shrink from five to **three** and plans to specialise in quality.
He remembers the earlier switch to online ordering and gains confidence from it.
He worries about younger staff doing only data entry.

steps.text: Take every course the wholesaler offers and use AI tools daily
Train as a quality inspector for fresh produce
Start a small side income with Selin, such as a weekend market stall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we've got to talk to the owners now, because we've nothing ready. Online I'd stay quiet, since I don't know what to say, but I'd be reading every article I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the buying job goes. I don't see how a man on the phone beats something that's read every price in the world. The market hub's ground floor and the lorries stay human a bit longer, but I'm not a lorry driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd cut spending to the bone. I'd ask my boss for a move into the warehouse side or quality, which is hands-on, so I last until the robots come. I'd look at my cousin's catering business as somewhere to land, and ask Selin's parents about help if the worst happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Not the loud kind, but sick in the stomach. I'm a provider, and I'd feel I'd let them down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years, then thinking work goes first. What does your own working life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight. I'd say my kind of job might be gone within two years, and here's what we do: cut this, save that, here's my cousin's offer. She'd say, we'll manage, and mean it, and I'd cry a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell Selin that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of time, yes. Robots do the heavy lifting around 2031, so a quality inspector or warehouse lead might have until then. It's not a rescue, but it's a landing.

say: I'd say we must talk to the **owners** now because nothing's ready.
Online I'd stay quiet but read every **article** I find.
think: The buying job goes: I don't see how a man on the phone beats something that has read **every price**.
The market floor and lorries stay human longer, but I'm not a lorry driver.
do: Ask my boss for a move into **quality** or warehouse work, which is hands-on.
Talk to my cousin about his catering business as a landing place.
feel: **Frightened**, sick in the stomach; as the provider I'd feel I'd let them down.
S2.quote: I don't see how a man on the phone beats something that's read every price in the world.
fieldNote: Hassan expects the buying role to **disappear** and moves quickly to hands-on roles.
He reaches for family: his cousin's catering and Selin's parents.
He sees himself as provider and feels the weight.

steps.text: Cut household spending to the bone from the first month
Ask to move into quality inspection or warehouse lead work
Ask Selin's parents about help if the worst happens
Work weekends at his cousin's catering business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's tight but doable, and I'd tell colleagues not to waste it. At work I'd say let's agree a plan with the owners. Online I'd say governments should fund retraining in places like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel uneasy but able to act. Steady's my style: I'd watch the first firms to change, then follow when it's proven. The risk is I wait one year too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd move to the quality side part-time to see if I like it, and get certified in food safety. I'd use AI every day to learn its limits. And I'd get savings to two months, then three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a spine. It feels like a long slope I can walk down rather than fall off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what do you do differently in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few years lets me build a cushion, which I've never had, and my son Deniz will be eighteen by then. I'd want my son to see me retraining, not hiding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the five-year timing that helps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the big supermarket buyers. If they switch to machines, we're next within a year. That's my signal.

I'd say governments should fund retraining in places like ours.
think: Steady is my style: I watch the first firms and follow once it's **proven**.
The risk is I wait one year too long.
do: Move to the **quality** side part-time and get a food safety certificate.
Use AI daily to learn its **limits**.
Build savings to two months, then three.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a spine; a slope I can walk down rather than fall off.
S3.quote: I'd want my son to see me retraining, not hiding.
fieldNote: Hassan's **steady** style is both his strength and his risk: he follows rather than leads.
His signal for acting is when supermarket buyers switch to machines.
He wants his son to see him adapt.

steps.text: Get a food safety certificate and shadow the quality team
Use AI every day to learn what it gets wrong
Build savings to three months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and not to get wound up. At work I'd tell the team to stay curious. Online I'd say nothing, because by then we'd have seen how it all goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm fine on my own work and a little anxious about the bills. The mortgage and the kids' costs are real now. I'd be fifty-three with Deniz and Aylin grown and the house mostly mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and use AI as it improves. I'd set aside money for a small share in my cousin's catering business. I'd learn quality control properly, and by year five I'd decide whether to move across.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years takes the edge off, but I'd still have moments where I'd look at the bills and swallow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is there anything you'd do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the machine and the market. Spend a month at five in the morning on the pallets, and then a month with the data. Don't be the person who only knows one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger buyers coming into the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long horizon gives room for mistakes. If I pick the wrong course, I've time to try another.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so don't get **wound up**.
I'd tell the team to stay **curious**.
think: I'm fine on my own work and a little anxious about the **bills**.
By 2036 the kids are grown and the house is mostly mine.
do: Keep working and use AI as it improves.
Put money into a small **share** of my cousin's catering business.
Learn quality control properly and decide by year five whether to **move across**.
feel: **Calm** mostly, but I'd still look at the bills and swallow.
S4.quote: Spend a month at five in the morning on the pallets, and then a month with the data. Don't be the person who only knows one.
fieldNote: Ten years softens things, but the **bills** keep Hassan anxious.
He would tell younger buyers to learn both the market floor and the data.
He treats the long horizon as room to make mistakes.

steps.text: Keep buying and use AI tools as they improve
Put money into a small share of the cousin's catering business
Learn quality control properly over the next five years
Stay in the job while deciding in year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can't get a cushion in that time, and I'm the sort who waits for things to be proven. What would help is early warning from the wholesaler, paid training and a government that funds retraining, so I'm not doing it with my own thin savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that a lot of us in the middle aren't shouting. We're getting up at five, paying the mortgage and hoping somebody sensible is in charge. That quiet group is bigger than people think.

headlineQuote: We're getting up at five, paying the mortgage and hoping somebody sensible is in charge. That quiet group is bigger than people think.
portrait: Hassan Yilmaz, 43, buys fresh and dried **produce** for a market-hub wholesaler, with a school-office wife, two kids and a heavy mortgage.
He's centrist and **steady**: he uses AI a few times a week and follows technology once it's proven.
Thin savings, a bonus tied to harvests and few local employers keep him uneasy even when little changes.
In faster scenarios he expects buying to shrink and plans to move to **quality** or warehouse work.
He copes through family: his cousin's catering and Selin's steady job.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because his wait-and-see style leaves him no time to build a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Early **warning** from the wholesaler, paid training and public funding for retraining.
